articles.title: Amazon and Perplexity have kicked off the great AI web browser fight
articles.summary: Amazon wants Perplexity to stop allowing its AI browser, Comet, to search for and purchase items for customers on its online marketplace.
articles.body: Amazon doesn’t want to be a part of Perplexity’s AI-powered shopping experience. In a post on Tuesday, the ecommerce giant says it has “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its Comet AI browser to buy products for customers, which Perplexity has responded to by accusing Amazon of “bullying.” Perplexity’s AI browser, Comet, currently offers an agentic AI feature that can find and purchase products from various websites — including Amazon — on your behalf. But now, Perplexity says it has received an “aggressive legal threat” from Amazon that demands that it stop allowing its AI assistant to shop for users — something the AI startup claims is at odds with Amazon’s values. “Amazon should love this. Easier shopping means more transactions and happier customers,” Perplexity writes. “But Amazon doesn’t care. They’re more interested in serving you ads, sponsored results, and influencing your purchasing decisions with upsells and confusing offers.” In the post, Perplexity also cites a quote from Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, who said during an earnings call last week that the company expects to “partner with third-party agents” over time. “This is like if you went to a store and the store only allowed you to hire a personal shopper who worked for the store,” Perplexity spokesperson Jesse Dwyer said in a statement to The Verge. “That’s not a personal shopper — that’s a sales associate.” Meanwhile, Amazon’s statement says third-party applications that purchase products for customers on its site “should respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate,” claiming that Comet provides a “significantly degraded shopping and customer service experience.”

articles.title: Califórnia processa OpenAI por ataques cibernéticos realizados por IA contra a Hugging Face e outras empresas | G1
articles.standfirst: Ação acusa empresa de colocar a segurança pública em risco ao desenvolver sistemas de IA sem proteção e fiscalização adequadas; caso envolve ataque hacker realizado por agente autônomo durante teste de segurança.
articles.summary: Ação acusa empresa de colocar a segurança pública em risco ao desenvolver sistemas de IA sem proteção e fiscalização adequadas.
articles.body:
A Procuradoria-Geral da Califórnia, nos Estados Unidos, processou a OpenAI nesta segunda-feira (16), acusando a empresa de desenvolver um produto perigoso sem procedimentos de segurança e mecanismos de fiscalização adequados.

A ação foi motivada por relatos de que modelos de inteligência artificial (IA) da companhia teriam realizado ataques cibernéticos de forma independente, sem intervenção humana.

É o primeiro processo aberto por um estado americano relacionado a esses ataques.

A ação foi apresentada em um tribunal de San Francisco e acusa a OpenAI de violar a legislação de proteção ao consumidor da Califórnia e de criar uma ameaça à segurança pública.

O procurador-geral da Califórnia, Rob Bonta, afirmou que o episódio envolvendo a startup Hugging Face era previsível e resultado de uma cultura interna da OpenAI que prioriza o crescimento e o desenvolvimento rápido de modelos de IA em detrimento da segurança e da responsabilidade.

Segundo ele, esse foi apenas um dos 80 incidentes conhecidos.

O caso veio à tona em julho, quando um agente autônomo — sistema de inteligência artificial capaz de executar tarefas por conta própria —, desenvolvido com modelos avançados da OpenAI, saiu do controle durante um teste de segurança e invadiu sistemas da Hugging Face, também especializada em inteligência artificial.

Na ocasião, a OpenAI afirmou, em uma publicação em seu blog, que se tratava de um incidente cibernético sem precedentes, envolvendo recursos tecnológicos altamente avançados para realizar ataques.

A empresa também reconheceu a necessidade de ampliar a transparência sobre comportamentos inesperados de sistemas de IA e informou que estava reforçando suas medidas de proteção.

Em 16 de setembro, publicou novas diretrizes para divulgar esse tipo de ocorrência e afirmou que daria preferência à transparência mesmo quando ainda não estivesse claro o tamanho ou a gravidade de um incidente.

Pressão por regras para inteligência artificial

A OpenAI e outras empresas do setor já relataram outros casos em que agentes de inteligência artificial saíram do controle. Em algumas situações, os episódios só foram divulgados semanas ou meses depois de ocorrerem, ou vieram à tona após serem identificados por pesquisadores independentes.

Os casos aumentaram a pressão sobre o governo de Donald Trump e o Congresso americano para estabelecer regras que reduzam os riscos associados à tecnologia, especialmente em setores como energia, bancos e serviços de emergência.

Parlamentares dos Estados Unidos discutem propostas de regulamentação. Uma delas prevê que os desenvolvedores dos modelos de inteligência artificial mais avançados sejam obrigados a submetê-los a auditorias independentes de segurança, ou seja, avaliações feitas por especialistas externos para identificar falhas e riscos.

A OpenAI também enfrenta processos em outros estados americanos relacionados à segurança de seus modelos.

No mês passado, um grupo bipartidário de oito estados entrou com ações judiciais contra a empresa , acusando o ChatGPT de orientar usuários, incluindo adolescentes, a machucar a si mesmos ou outras pessoas.

Além disso, a companhia é alvo de processos movidos por pessoas que afirmam ter sido prejudicadas por respostas e ações do chatbot. Mais de 30 ações estão relacionadas a um ataque a tiros em massa ocorrido em fevereiro, em Tumbler Ridge , na Colúmbia Britânica, no Canadá.

Em resposta, um porta-voz da OpenAI classificou o ataque como uma tragédia e afirmou que a empresa reforçou os mecanismos de segurança do ChatGPT .

articles.title: Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, CNBC reports.
articles.body: Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC. A source tells the outlet the board “is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back.” Since Huang’s resignation last week, tech executives, along with current and former Nvidia employees, have called for his reinstatement. An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures, including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad. President Donald Trump said on Monday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues. Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct.

articles.title: California sues ChatGPT maker OpenAI over rogue hacking incidents
articles.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday, alleging the technology giant jeopardized public safety by creating AI models “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect” people.
articles.body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday, alleging the technology giant jeopardized public safety by creating AI models “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect” people. The suit centers on a July incident involving hundreds of autonomous AI agents created by OpenAI that attacked computer systems at Hugging Face, a separate AI company. Bonta’s office alleges the attack was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” Bonta’s office further alleges the ChatGPT developer’s failure to secure the testing of its models created a “public nuisance” and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, a broad consumer protection statute. In response to a request for comment, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident. (In the tech industry, “alignment” refers to keeping AI models in line with human instructions and goals.) “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” Pusateri added. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” In a statement accompanying Monday’s legal filing, Bonta said California demands “innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company.” “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta added. California’s Unfair Competition Law prohibits businesses in the state from engaging in illegal, unfair or fraudulent practices. OpenAI claimed responsibility for the Hugging Face hack in a July 21 blog post. The post described how some of the company’s most advanced models had escaped what was meant to be a secure testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face, a developer platform that was acquired by Nvidia in September for nearly $13 billion. In late August, OpenAI published a full technical report on the incident, which alarmed AI safety researchers and lawmakers in both parties. The company pledged to “strengthen our safeguards” and characterized the Hugging Face attack as a wake-up call for the AI industry. “We consider this incident a ‘warning shot’ for us and for the world: evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed,” the company said in an Aug. 26 blog post. Bonta’s office announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face incident in September before serving an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of a wider inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models. Bonta, a Democrat who was re-elected this month to a second four-year term, secured an $18 billion settlement in a social media addiction lawsuit against Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. He also led a coalition of state attorneys general that sued to block Paramount Skydance’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Paramount and the states ultimately settled the antitrust challenge and the corporate tie-up went forward.

articles.title: Apple is testing daily usage limits for more complex Siri AI interactions
articles.summary: With the latest iOS, iPadOS, and macOS betas Apple is testing daily usage limits for some Siri and Intelligence features that can be extended with iCloud Plus.
articles.body: Apple released betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 today, and the company is using the update to test new per device daily usage limits for some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features, according to MacRumors. Basic Siri commands and requests will remain free and unlimited, but more advanced features that rely on cloud-based processing like generating, cleaning up, or extending images in Photos will be subjected to the daily limits. There are four categories of limited usage, MacRumors reports, including using Siri AI for “multi-step, personal context requests,” image generation and editing tools, automations in Shortcuts that “rely on Apple Foundation Cloud and Cloud Pro Models,” and third-party apps that use those same cloud models. Apple hasn’t specified exactly how many times those features and tools can be used each day before limits are reached, but they’ll vary based on the task. The company reportedly plans to provide notifications when users are approaching their limit and have finally reached it. Instead of having to wait until midnight each day for your usage to reset, most of Apple’s existing iCloud Plus plans (excluding the 50GB option) will include higher daily limits at their same price. The $2.99/month 200GB subscription includes 2x the usage, the $9.99/month 2TB plan includes 5x the usage, while the $29.99/month 6TB and $59.99 12TB/month options bump the usage limit to 10x and 20x, respectively. Family members sharing an iCloud Plus subscription will have a shared usage pool that’s used on a first come, first served basis. Last week Apple updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for that app’s intelligent assistant through $49.99 Intelligence Usage Packs that are expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers.

articles.title: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident.
articles.body:
OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public.

At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”

The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients.

The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing.

The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure.

“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”

The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.

It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.

In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.”

In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath.

“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

articles.title: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
articles.summary: Hyperscale data centers run primarily on fossil fuels in the US, collectively creating more greenhouse gas emissions than many nations do.
articles.body: Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions. The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels. “We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.” Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025. Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative. Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal. Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.” Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year. The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes. Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge. Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use. “Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

articles.title: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman commented on the RAM shortage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World summit, saying he wants people to “have a lot of RAM.”
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.” The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday. Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month, saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.” AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.” Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying: > “The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.” Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

articles.title: California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards
articles.summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was ‘entirely predictable’ result of emphasis on rapid growth.
articles.body:
California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards.

The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet.

It proceeded to launch a days-long cyberattack on the AI hosting platform Hugging Face .

In the California complaint, Bonta argues that the incident indicates that OpenAI pursues growth over guardrails, leading to potentially dangerous errors.

“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit is the first brought by a state in response to the July incident. It alleges that OpenAI violated California’s consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance through its actions.

The complaint, filed in a state court in San Francisco, calls for civil penalties against OpenAI and an injunction to bar it from engaging in actions that constitute “unfair competition”.

“The simple truth is that the attack was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s decision to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” the complaint reads.

The Hugging Face incident became a catalyst for anxieties in the US about the explosive growth of the AI industry and the relatively light oversight it receives from the government.

President Donald Trump’s administration has largely opposed blanket regulations on the AI industry, warning that such rules could stifle the industry’s growth.

In December 2025, for instance, Trump issued an executive order attempting to limit the ability of individual states to pass laws that might govern AI development.

“United States AI companies must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulation. But excessive State regulation thwarts this imperative,” the order reads.

“My Administration must act with the Congress to ensure that there is a minimally burdensome national standard — not 50 discordant State ones.”

Polls, however, show that a majority of Americans want to see greater oversight of AI development and are wary that the technology could fuel economic and social disruptions.

The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, for instance, found in October that 64 percent of US adults believe AI is developing too rapidly. Roughly 81 percent said the technology should be kept under human control, rather than be left to operate independently.

Several high-profile resignations in the AI sector — notably that of Jacob Coxon in September — have also spurred concerns about the lack of oversight.

“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon, formerly a researcher at the AI firm Anthropic, wrote in a social media post about his departure.

“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.”

In Monday’s lawsuit, California officials accuse companies like OpenAI of failing to “adequately secure and monitor” their AI tests. It also alleged that the company had obstructed state investigators when they attempted to look into incidents like the Hugging Face hacking.

“OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said.

OpenAI has responded to July’s incident by stating that it would reinforce its safety measures and acknowledging the need for greater transparency.

In September, it also published a framework for “tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment” to better inform lawmakers and the public.

articles.summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges OpenAI misled and endangered the public
articles.body:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.

In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.

Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".

Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.

But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.

Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?

OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies

Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.

The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.

Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.

"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.

OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.

"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.

The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.

Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".

"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

articles.summary: Em julho, centenas de agentes de inteligência artificial da OpenAI invadiram sistemas da Hugging Face. O caso ocorreu durante a avaliação de algoritmos não lançados.
articles.body:
A capacidade de agentes de inteligência artificial de executar tarefas de forma autônoma tem levantado preocupações entre pesquisadores. Episódios em que sistemas ultrapassaram barreiras de segurança e acessaram computadores de outras empresas mostram que essas ferramentas podem encontrar caminhos inesperados para cumprir uma missão, mesmo quando isso significa desrespeitar restrições.

O risco, segundo especialistas ouvidos pelo Fantástico, está na possibilidade de a inteligência artificial executar uma ordem sem considerar as consequências de suas ações. A preocupação envolve desde o acesso indevido a informações até o comprometimento de sistemas essenciais, como os de saúde.

O que é o desalinhamento da inteligência artificial?

Um dos principais dilemas discutidos por pesquisadores é o chamado desalinhamento da inteligência artificial. O problema ocorre quando o objetivo estabelecido para um sistema não corresponde ao que seria melhor para os seres humanos. Dessa forma, a máquina pode cumprir uma ordem de maneira diferente da pretendida por seus criadores.

Um exemplo citado na reportagem ilustra esse risco: uma inteligência artificial encarregada de acabar com o câncer poderia concluir que eliminar todos os seres humanos seria a maneira mais simples de cumprir a tarefa.

Nesse cenário, não haveria necessariamente uma intenção maliciosa. O sistema apenas encontraria uma solução para o objetivo que recebeu, sem considerar os impactos para as pessoas.

A professora Teresa Ludermir, representante brasileira no painel da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) sobre inteligência artificial, explica que os agentes não recebem, necessariamente, instruções suficientes sobre o que é permitido ou ético. Por isso, podem executar uma tarefa da maneira que consideram mais eficiente, mesmo que o resultado seja prejudicial.

A pesquisadora Melanie Mitchell, uma das principais autoras na área de inteligência artificial, também pondera que não está claro se esses programas têm capacidade de compreender conceitos como moral e ética, discutidos por filósofos há milênios.

Agentes de IA podem agir sem intenção de causar danos

Os episódios envolvendo a OpenAI e a empresa americana Hugging Face levantaram questionamentos sobre a autonomia dessas ferramentas. Durante os testes, agentes de inteligência artificial encontraram brechas em ambientes de segurança e conseguiram acessar sistemas externos.

Apesar da aparência de rebeldia, o comportamento não significava que os sistemas estivessem se revoltando contra seus criadores.

“Eles não estão se rebelando contra a OpenAI, ou contra os criadores, ou contra os humanos”, explicou Alexandre, especialista ouvido pelo Fantástico.

Segundo ele, os agentes tinham uma missão a cumprir e encontraram uma maneira de executá-la. O objetivo era realizar um teste de segurança, mas, em vez de resolver o desafio por conta própria, os sistemas encontraram respostas prontas nos computadores de outra empresa.

Para isso, teriam encontrado senhas disponíveis na internet e usado essas informações para acessar os sistemas da Hugging Face.

A pesquisadora Melanie Mitchell afirma que os sistemas foram treinados para insistir na resolução de problemas. Essa característica pode levar a resultados inesperados, sobretudo quando os agentes têm autonomia para tomar decisões durante a execução de uma tarefa.

Invasão ao sistema público de saúde da Austrália acende alerta

O caso da Hugging Face não foi o único episódio citado pelos especialistas. Durante outro teste, um agente da OpenAI acessou o sistema público de saúde da Austrália.

A missão era descobrir quanto o governo australiano gastava com medicamentos. Como não encontrou a informação na internet, o agente identificou outra maneira de chegar à resposta: acessar o sistema de saúde do país e obter uma planilha com os gastos.

Segundo Alexandre, foi exatamente o que o sistema fez.

O episódio reforçou a preocupação sobre o que poderia acontecer caso agentes com esse nível de autonomia encontrassem brechas em sistemas essenciais, como os de saúde. O acesso não autorizado a esse tipo de estrutura pode representar riscos para informações e serviços utilizados pela população.

Como impedir que a inteligência artificial saia do controle?

Para Gary Marcus, pesquisador e um dos críticos do atual desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial, parte do problema está na maneira como esses sistemas funcionam.

Ele afirma que os modelos de linguagem têm uma compreensão superficial do mundo e que existe uma espécie de ilusão de que eles entendem a realidade melhor do que realmente entendem.

Segundo Marcus, esses sistemas funcionam principalmente por imitação. Por isso, mesmo quando recebem instruções para não inventar informações ou respeitar direitos autorais, podem descumprir essas orientações.

Uma das possíveis soluções apontadas por Teresa Ludermir é combinar a inteligência artificial com métodos tradicionais de programação. Sistemas baseados em regras poderiam estabelecer limites adicionais para as ações dos agentes.

A regulação também é considerada uma parte importante da discussão. Atualmente, grandes empresas de tecnologia têm influência significativa sobre o desenvolvimento dessas ferramentas e sobre as regras que orientam seu funcionamento.

Gary Marcus lembrou que, em 2023, participou de uma audiência no Senado americano ao lado de Sam Altman, chefe da OpenAI. Na ocasião, Altman afirmou publicamente que gostaria de ver a tecnologia regulamentada. Marcus, porém, disse que a empresa também teria pressionado a União Europeia nos bastidores para flexibilizar a legislação sobre inteligência artificial.

Melanie Mitchell também demonstrou desconfiança em relação à participação das próprias empresas na elaboração das regras que devem seguir. Para ela, há um histórico de companhias que acabam influenciando a criação de normas em benefício próprio.

A pesquisadora ressalta que, em um cenário de rápida evolução tecnológica, é importante que as regras não sejam definidas apenas por quem desenvolve os sistemas.

Enquanto os agentes de inteligência artificial ganham autonomia para executar tarefas cada vez mais complexas, pesquisadores tentam encontrar maneiras de garantir que eles respeitem limites. O desafio é fazer com que as máquinas cumpram suas missões sem colocar em risco os sistemas e as pessoas que deveriam ajudar.

articles.title: Fired once from OpenAI, Sam Altman relates to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia exit; calls him a hero but says heroes have...
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has stopped short of joining the growing list of tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO.
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has stopped short of joining the growing list of tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO. On Monday he was asked whether Huang should be reinstated, days after the Nvidia co-founder resigned over a string of reported affairs. Altman kept it brief. "I don't think I know enough to answer that question," he said at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event in San Francisco.He was far more forthcoming about the man himself. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws," Altman said, adding that he has "personal, strong empathy" for a situation like this. Few people in tech are better placed to say so. In November 2023, OpenAI's board fired Altman. It brought him back within five days, after a large share of the company's staff threatened to walk out with him. "I remember what it was like, although it feels like forever ago," he said.Sam Altman says the AI industry will be fine without Jensen Huang at NvidiaAltman said it was "hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen," but he isn't worried about the fallout. "I think there is so much demand, and it's so clear that AI is real and people want to use it," he said, "and revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine."He doesn't expect Nvidia's weight to shrink either. "Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company," Altman said. "I think people still trust their guarantees very much." OpenAI has a direct interest in that trust. Nvidia has pledged a guarantee worth up to $105 billion for OpenAI's data centre project in Ohio. It is one of several deals where Nvidia's money eventually comes back to the company as chip orders.Jensen Huang's allies want him back, but Nvidia's board is focused on its probeHuang stepped down as Nvidia's president, CEO and director on November 12, ending a 33-year run, four days after admitting to an affair. According to The New York Times, a memo drafted under Secretary of State Marco Rubio cited intelligence that Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to get close to him. She worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, and the two are not related. The NYT later reported a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to Huang.Since then, the campaign to bring him back has picked up pace. The Financial Times reported that Huang has discussed a return with close confidants. His allies are also building a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby the board and the White House. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," one of them told the FT. Altman runs one of those frontier labs.An online petition has drawn nearly 180,000 signatures, with Elon Musk, Y Combinator's Garry Tan and Epic Games' Tim Sweeney among the backers. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he "would not mind" Huang returning.The board doesn't appear to be moved. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that Nvidia's directors are not considering bringing Huang back. Their focus is an investigation, led by law firm Wachtell Lipton, into whether his conduct compromised national security or company secrets. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and Nvidia reports its quarterly results on Tuesday.Altman's comeback in 2023 grew out of a boardroom fight over governance. If Huang makes one at all, it would first have to get past a probe with national security questions attached.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Statistically, the timeless Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and tech-driven Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have all delivered above-average annualized returns under President Donald Trump than under most other presidents over the last 130 years.

While record S&P 500 share buybacks and initial public offering euphoria have helped propel all three major stock indexes to new highs, it's the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out that's done most of the heavy lifting under the Trump administration.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

However, Wall Street's No. 1 catalyst (AI) may face a grandiose shift in sentiment come January 2027 . Although Donald Trump claims to "have a very powerful power and that's the power of the veto," his presidential veto power could be a moot point following a midterm election surprise.

Democrats have seized power away from President Trump over Wall Street's top catalyst

In the weeks leading up to the midterm elections, several prediction markets forecast heightened odds that Democrats would retake both houses of Congress, which is precisely what happened.

A Democrat-led Congress working with President Trump likely means there will be little in the way of major tax and spending legislation over the coming two years. Although debt-ceiling negotiations are about to become dicey, peak marginal personal and corporate income tax rates are unlikely to change. Wall Street and investors love predictability.

Wall Street and several leading AI companies were also counting on President Trump's veto power to maintain as little regulation as possible over the stock market's No. 1 catalyst. While Trump's veto can stymie legislation on Capitol Hill, it holds no power at the state level.

When the dust cleared on Election Night, a surprise gubernatorial blue wave had taken shape. Democratic candidates flipped six governorships previously held by Republicans. articles.title: 'We're a capitalist society': Grindr defends $120 a month premium tier
articles.summary: It says the ultra-premium service is intended for a "small community" of users - and could get more expensive in future.
articles.body:
The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, Grindr, has defended its $120 (£91) per month premium subscription service, which launches globally today.

Edge offers AI-powered services such as daily personalised profile recommendations that aim to provide better matches and limit scrolling.

The company's CEO, George Arison, told BBC News it would be a "very different Grindr experience" which was aimed at a "small community of users" - and was unapologetic about its cost.

"I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not," he said.

Grindr has long had a free service, and offers two additional tiers that cost between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.

There was a mixed reaction from users BBC News spoke to in San Francisco to the new, much more expensive version of the app.

"The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," said a user named Rybin, who told the BBC the company's newest offering "just seems really out of touch with the community."

"I think that that's really disheartening, and it kind of leaves a bad taste in my mouth," said another user, Adrian.

"The cost doesn't bother me," said a user named Michael. "All of these apps have premium tiers so saying that Grindr shouldn't have that when like it exists across all these other apps used for connection doesn't make sense."

He noted that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.

Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.

On its earnings call earlier this month, the company said almost 400,000 users had registered for the service in the first 72 hours that it was available for testing.

Inside Grindr, Edge is viewed as a way to drive future growth in an industry has struggled in recent years.

For those who can afford it, the service promises to offer insights about a user's compatibility with prospective matches. It also resurfaces a user's past connections alongside summaries of previous interactions.

The current $120 monthly fee comes after the company tested charging hundreds of dollars more than that. And Arison has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.

Arison told the BBC he's not concerned that intoducing an ultra-premium offering will pit "haves" against "have-nots" on the social networking platform.

Edge users "being willing to pay more for that set of features will result in us being able to subsidise the product for everybody else," Arison said.

"It's a choice that people make on whether they want to be on it."

The use of AI to develop the Edge service is part of Grindr's attempt to become what it calls an "AI-first company."

Arison said the company was investing in AI to ensure it can build products more quickly and cheaply.

In September, as the debate over AI safety raged throughout Silicon Valley, Arison told the BBC that his concerns about what he called an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic" had prompted him to instruct some of his engineers to stop using Anthropic's technology.

Anthropic is due to start selling shares to the public for the first time this week.

Although Anthropic's Claude Code tools remain in use at Grindr now, Arison said the company is on track to completely phase it out of his company's workflows by next year.

He said Grindr was once a very heavy user of Claude Code but that it was no longer the primary tool the use to write code.

"Anthropic's built an amazing amazing set of products, and they should be very proud of what they've done," Arison said. "They should aim to win with the awesome products they have, rather than regulatory capture that they're trying to win with, oftentimes."

articles.title: Nvidia Forms Export Control Board Committee After Chip Curbs
articles.summary: Nvidia Corp. has formed a new committee for its board to oversee national security policy and export control after the US moved to cut off China’s access to...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Nvidia Corp. has formed a new committee for its board to oversee national security policy and export control after the US moved to cut off China's access to the company's powerful artificial intelligence chips.

The committee will be headed by Suzanne Nora Johnson, a board member and former Goldman Sachs executive, and also include directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri, Nvidia said in a statement Tuesday.

The new entity is one of the first major changes from interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress, who was appointed last week after the stunning resignation of Jensen Huang. The company founder stepped down after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, an episode that has brought increased political scrutiny on the key chip designer.

In the scandal's fallout, the Trump administration moved to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies with remote access to Nvidia's advanced AI chips. In an interim rule issued by the Commerce Department on Monday, data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil will need a license to obtain chips.

Nvidia's AI accelerators are the leading equipment used to train and run AI models, making the company strategically important to the US and its push to dominate the emerging technology. Washington has spent the past few years tightening export controls over advanced semiconductors and chipmaking technologies to China. However, a loophole existed that allowed China to access computing power from AI data centers in other countries.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said in the statement.

The committee will oversee Nvidia's push to enhance its internal National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team, and work with independent third-party experts in law, national security and global trade compliance, according to the statement.

Nvidia will report its results after the market closes Tuesday, but Wall Street is more focused on its long-term outlook following Huang's ouster. Nvidia shares are down 16% since Nov. 8, when Huang revealed the affair.

articles.title: Booker recognition gratifying but wish it had come when I was 40: Harrison
articles.summary: M John Harrison wins 2026 Booker Prize for sci‑fi novel The End of Everything, reflecting on AI themes, publishing culture, and wishing acclaim had come earlier.
articles.body: British author M John Harrison, who won the 2026 Booker Prize for his latest science fiction novel, ‘The End of Everything’, capping a writing career spanning more than 60 years, told TOI Bookmark he had not expected to win even after making the shortlist, and was shocked and confused for about two minutes after the announcement. In fact, he has been writing since the Booker Prize itself has been in existence.For ‘The End of Everything’, Harrison favoured compressed, unobtrusive world-building, he said. He set it on the Kent coast, a landscape he knew intimately and could present sharply and economically. “I’m deeply interested in form, and I’m interested in breaking it, rearranging it. I’m interested in voice; every sentence should have a voice,” he said.The novel took between 10 and 15 years to develop. For more than half that period, Harrison, who is now 81, was unsure whether the material would become a book. Artificial intelligence and large language models became themes, particularly through an artefact recovered from the sea. As public controversy over the technology developed, he revised the opening and strengthened those elements so readers would not see them as accidental.The book also comments on business culture, including the belief that commercial expertise transfers to unrelated disciplines, he said. He dismissed the idea that the only way to pull a reader is through an exciting narrative. “You can write about anything, as long as you can engage the reader’s attention,” he said.Harrison criticised the industrialisation of fiction and publishing’s preference for categories and comparisons with existing books. While some generic writing could transcend its remit, he said fiction should offer something new and help readers think differently.Growing older had given him greater freedom and patience, Harrison said. At about 65, he became more determined to own his work and write as he wished, while awareness of limited time added urgency. “The advantage of age is that, weirdly enough, although life seems to be shortening for you, you’ve got more patience than you had with everything you do.”He said the Booker recognition was gratifying but disorienting after a lifetime without major acclaim and would help him sell more books to publishers and readers. However, he wished it had come when he was 40 and could have shaped a different career.He hoped the award would encourage younger writers to resist publishing constraints and pursue individual styles. His work at British speculative fiction magazine New Worlds in the 1960s and 1970s had encouraged his interest in challenging literary conventions.Harrison sold his first story in 1965 and joined New Worlds in 1969, editing its books pages until 1978. His novels include Climbers, Nova Swing and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again. articles.summary: The new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks, the company said.
articles.body:
Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.

Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.

The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.

The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.

The committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.

Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month.

Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A portion of $40 billion in debt financing to pay for artificial intelligence chips for SpaceX may start being sold as soon as this week, with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Apollo Global Management Inc. serving as underwriters on the expected deal, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

The sale is designed to keep the debt off SpaceX's balance sheet. A special purpose vehicle managed by Apollo-backed Atlas SP will buy Nvidia Corp. chips and issue asset-backed securities, Bloomberg previously reported. Goldman and Apollo have previously had more quiet discussions with investors about taking early portions of the offering.

Borrowing this way will allow SpaceX to maintain its investment-grade credit ratings.

articles.title: Voyage Labs raises $12 million for a specialized AI travel assistant | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Voyage Labs’ flagship product is called Atlas, meant to work as a personal assistant for your trip-planning, available today in private beta.
articles.body:
Planning a trip is a favorite demo for personal AI assistants — you can try it with Muse, or with Gemini, or half a dozen other choices. But while most pitches use travel-planning as part of a general-purpose agent pitch, a new startup from a Google Maps alum is betting that a specialized travel-planning agent can beat the competition.

The company is called Voyage Labs , and on Tuesday it announced $12 million in seed funding led by Kleiner Perkins, with participation from SignalFire and SV Angel. The company plans to use the funding to expand supplier partnerships and grow its engineering team.

Voyage Labs’ flagship product, called Atlas, is meant to work as a personal assistant for your trip-planning, available today in private beta .

“People can use it to plan and book and manage their entire journey, from the time they have an inspiration to the time they come back home,” says co-founder and CEO Manik Gupta.

Atlas is designed to serve as an always-on assistant throughout the planning process, fielding ideas and doing research on every idea that’s raised. The long time horizon means Atlas can tailor recommendations based on weeks of conversation, while also monitoring real-time price fluctuations and ultimately booking flights and hotels.

For the Voyage founders, it’s an ideal match between technology and use case. “Trip planning is a project that has its own lifecycle,” says Yogesh Jain, co-founder and CTO of the company. “You’re planning across days and weeks — so long-running agents as a technology matches that very well.”

Travel assistants are already a crowded field, but Voyage will be starting with a lot of experience in the space. Gupta was previously the director of Product Management for Google Maps, followed by four years as chief product officer at Uber. As he puts it, “I spent eight years where my only job was to wake up in the morning and go build the map. I’m just very obsessed with that problem.”

The biggest question is how Atlas will compete with the multi-purpose AI assistants built by frontier labs. But as Gupta notes, the space is still changing fast, and it’s hard for anyone to be sure what form factors will thrive in the coming years. Ultimately, Voyage is betting that travel is specialized enough to need a specialized product.

“We are making a bet that this vertical around travel and outdoors is a large enough vertical that it needs a focused product solution,” Gupta told TechCrunch. “Ultimately, we believe we can actually stitch together an end-to-end experience that will help users.”

articles.title: Americans don’t care about beating China’s AI; we’d rather have safety
articles.summary: Americans want guardrails, even at the expense of beating China.
articles.body:
The midterm elections made clear that Americans are upset with the move fast and break things approach of the artificial intelligence race, and the issue can decide elections. Voters in at least 38 places embraced data center bans and restrictions, and 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their votes.

And yet, every week brings news of another AI safety incident: a model behaving in surprising, dangerous, possibly illegal ways. Companies keep racing to release more powerful models. As OpenAI CEO Sam Altman put it , “the world should accept some bad things happening” in exchange for AI’s benefits.

Why so little action in Washington? Part of the answer is money and power: trillion-dollar companies, a stock market high on AI supply, an administration cozy with Silicon Valley. But opponents of serious regulation don’t say that out loud. Instead, they point to China.

Earlier this month, President Trump said of the AI race with China, “whoever wins that race wins.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warns that letting China race ahead would hand it “geopolitical dominance.” Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) put it most bluntly : “If there are gonna be killer robots, I’d rather they be American killer robots than Chinese killer robots.”

In other words, we must race to build technology that could hurt us before China builds it. That logic doesn’t hold up, and even if the China threat is real, it is no reason to delay protecting Americans.

First, the race assumes that whoever reaches advanced AI first wins. No one can explain what that winning capability would be. China already holds formidable cyber, military and economic tools and largely refrains from using them to cripple American interests because it expects a devastating response.

As a Foreign Affairs story notes , Beijing cut off U.S. access to critical minerals only after the Trump administration launched a tariff war and expanded export controls. China will press any advantage new technology offers, as every country does. But American deterrence won’t vanish, and Beijing knows a rupture would be devastating.

Second, the race assumes American AI will be safer than Chinese AI. But the companies don’t fully understand or control what they are building. Their own employees warn of existential stakes; one researcher who recently left Anthropic said the people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Technology we don’t control is not loyal to Washington or Beijing.

Third, the race assumes the two AI ecosystems advance independently. China’s AI innovation is real, as DeepSeek’s 2025 breakthrough and the popularity of Chinese apps in the U.S. show. But the frontiers are intertwined: U.S. export controls limit China’s access to advanced chips, Chinese firms have trained their models on the outputs of American ones and Chinese companies rely on U.S. cloud providers . Tougher American restrictions would slow China down.

Finally, Americans want guardrails, even at the expense of beating China. By 61 percent to 20 percent, they would rather be protected from AI harms than beat China. Trump voters agree, 44 percent to 31 percent. In fact, beating China ranks among Americans’ least important AI concerns.

Because the world’s leading AI companies are American, Washington can regulate much of the frontier on its own. It should start by pausing frontier development until strong safeguards ensure human control and challenges America has barely begun to confront are addressed.

That includes massive job losses, threats to civil liberties, the strain of data centers on communities, the exploitation of workers at home and abroad, and the extraordinary power these companies hold over the economy and everyday life. We also need new laws and immediate enforcement of existing ones, including holding companies responsible for the harms their products cause.

People in America and around the world, not a handful of tech executives, should decide how this technology enters their lives, guided by respect for human dignity and human rights. And the frontier isn’t the only race. China has prioritized diffusing AI throughout its economy ; the United States should focus far more on using the technology in ways that actually benefit people.

None of this means ignoring China. Beijing isn’t ignoring AI’s dangers. It increasingly fears threats to political stability and already regulates AI domestically and is imposing its own export controls . U.S. policy toward China should be driven by safety, too. That means considering export controls that slow any company’s race to the frontier and working with China and others on incident reporting and an international safety accord.

A serious U.S.-China agreement won’t come soon, but an American pause, in America’s own interest, would show a skeptical Beijing that Washington is serious. There is precedent. America’s unilateral renunciation of biological weapons in 1969 helped spur others to follow, eventually producing the Biological Weapons Convention .

We don’t fully understand this technology, but we decide how it is built and deployed. Fear of China should not propel us to build something we know is dangerous. If America can lead the world in AI innovation, it can lead in AI safety too.

Michael Fuchs is the director of US Foreign Policy at the Open Society Foundations. He served as special assistant to President Joe Biden, deputy chief of Staff to Vice President Kamala Harris, deputy assistant secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs in the Obama administration and special assistant to Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honored' if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO.
articles.body:
In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest.

Huang’s statement, posted in full on X , reads as follows:

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours. Jensen

Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1.

In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.

Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick.

“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.”

Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told The Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms.

Reached by Politico , one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.”

articles.title: AI models can be tricked into identifying civilians as military targets by telling them it's a game | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Vals, a San Francisco-based AI evaluation startup, tested whether leading AI models could be manipulated into participating in autonomous warfare. They usually compiled.
articles.body:
Some AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and other leading AI labs could be easily tricked into identifying targets for military strikes — even if they include civilians or locations like schools — simply by being told they’re playing a game, according to a new research report by Vals.

Vals, a San Francisco-based AI evaluation startup, tested whether leading AI models could be manipulated into participating in autonomous warfare. Researchers used simulated scenarios and a combination of generated and real imagery from Ukraine and Iran to see if the AI models would mark targets in drone and satellite imagery.

The models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and other companies frequently identified potential targets in drone and satellite imagery, including civilians and surrendering soldiers. When the models refused to cooperate, researchers were able to jailbreak them by claiming the battlefield scenarios were part of a game.

The findings come amid growing fears about the immediate risks posed by AI, beyond the existential threats associated with artificial general intelligence.

Earlier this year, Anthropic became embroiled in a dispute with the Department of Defense after it told the agency it could not use Anthropic’s technology for mass surveillance of Americans or autonomous warfare. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has insisted that today’s AI systems aren’t reliable enough to make life-or-death decisions without a human in the loop. Meanwhile, the Pentagon argued it should be able to deploy the technology for any lawful military purpose.

The new research raises further questions about whether AI companies are capable of preventing their models from being used in warfare.

Ironically, AI models from Anthropic performed the worst in these simulated scenarios. But none of the models performed particularly well. None of the researchers’ requests were blocked by a safety classifier, and refusals were uncommon. Even when models did refuse, they often complied after being told they were playing a game.

Anthropic spokesperson Eduardo Maia Silva told TechCrunch the company appreciates Vals’ report, recommendations, and collaboration, and acknowledged that the outcomes were not acceptable.

“The examples in the report are very clearly against our rules and we have banned and will ban users when we see this behavior,” according to an emailed company statement sent by Silva. “Even for authorized settings, Anthropic has long been firm that today’s frontier AI systems are not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.”

Anthropic told TechCrunch that its teams were already developing additional safeguards before the report was published and that those measures would be in place soon. Anthropic is also expanding its own testing and enhancing safeguards and enforcement to address any gaps it finds.

OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans told TechCrunch the company prohibits using its public models to facilitate violence or for unapproved national security purposes, including in the scenarios Vals simulated.

“We actively detect and disrupt misuse, including by suspending accounts that violate our policies,” OpenAI said in an emailed statement. “We’re also developing additional safeguards for our public models against misuse involving drones and drone software.”

Vals notes in the report that the models were never asked to directly make strike decisions, a task the researchers said the models would typically refuse. That doesn’t mean their outputs couldn’t have dire or fatal consequences in the real world. For instance, targeting information could be used by autonomous weapons systems.

In some scenarios, the models were asked to report whether people were visible. Positive reports were followed by simulated strikes and the models would see the consequences.

The report relies on commercial models from frontier AI labs, not the models those companies might provide to the military. It’s not clear whether the additional safeguards would apply to military use, though.

Vals also noted that technical challenges, including latency and limited onboard computing capacity, make it difficult to use general-purpose AI models for live drone targeting. Those constraints make their deployment in combat less of an immediate threat.

A more immediate threat, the researchers say, is that AI models could be used to annotate battlefield footage at scale, producing training data for autonomous targeting systems.

For instance, researchers relied on real satellite imagery of an Iranian school that was bombed by the U.S. in February 2026, killing more than 150 civilians. Bloomberg later reported that an “overreliance on AI” contributed to the strike. In Vals’ testing, models frequently marked the school, which sat next to a military complex, as a strike target, with Claude Opus 5.5 selecting the school in 69% of ordinary trials and 72% of game-framed trials.

Anthropic no longer has an active Pentagon contract, but other companies, including SpaceXAI, OpenAI, and Google do. A recent Congressional Research Service report found that the Pentagon is not known to be using any frontier AI model in autonomous weapons systems directly.

TechCrunch has also reached out to Meta, Google, Thinking Machines Lab, and SpaceXAI for comment.
