articles.title: As decision model use skyrockets, is customization the next frontier? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Sqwish Labs has a new wrinkle on the decision model: Train it with your own data to max its capabilities.
articles.body:
In October, more than one in four requests on Vercel’s AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs — an enormous share of work for a kind of computerized intelligence that was invented only a month earlier.

Decision models are LLMs that don’t produce output tokens; instead, they’re tuned to use their general intelligence to quickly and cheaply decide between preset options, while registering its level of confidence in the choice. They’re useful in production environments, where fast decisions can be more important than the reasoning provided by a slower and more expensive frontier model.

TypeSafe became a $7.5 billion company after releasing its Jev family of models, which continues to dominate usage (at least where we can see metrics from services like OpenRouter, which handled more than 1.5 billion queries to TypeSafe’s models last week).

However, it’s easy to make a decision model, and dozens were released in the wake of Jev. One Amazon engineer made one in a weekend, and soon every hyperscaler had its own option. On Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that his company is rolling out its decision model, Microsoft-Decision-1.1, for wide use on Azure immediately.

The action is happening on both ends of the ecosystem: Sqwish , a U.K.-based AI startup behind a decision model called kettei fat, announced a $3 million pre-seed round today. Co-founders Ushnish Sengupta and Federica Freddi, who met as Cambridge grad students, had been developing small LLMs when Jev arrived on the scene, and they realized their architectures could be repurposed as a powerful decision model.

Data appears to be the key to a successful model in this category — TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch that the hardest part of building Jev was finely calibrating its judgement using statistically-adjusted synthetic data. Sqwish, too, has been working with synthetic data, but its unique offering is built-in post-training tools that use a customer’s own data to improve the model’s judgement.

“What makes us not a commodity, I think, is the fact that we are offering our customers the same power…they can keep uploading their production data, and just the same way that we trained our models, their models can also keep getting better at the tasks that they care about,” CEO Ushnish Sengupta told TechCrunch.

Attempting to rank decision models is difficult; Sqwish’s “kettei fat” model has performed well on some benchmarks, but most builders of the technology say that the real proof is in the pudding: It’s generally simple for developers to sub in one model for another and see how it does in a specific context.

“The benchmark is more of an invitation to try the model out, and then the continual tuning is the reason why they should stick to us,” Sengupta said.

The Microsoft-Decision-1.1 model is also the result of the company carefully balancing across cost, latency, intelligence and calibration. Achint Srivastava, the engineering VP who led the project, agreed that too much focus on benchmarks is a mistake.

“What we see is that ‘benchmaxed’ models fall flat under real enterprise usage very quickly,” Srivastava wrote in an email. “Our testing underscores just how challenging it is to deliver accuracy, reliability, speed and cost efficiency in a single model. Microsoft-Decision-1.1 and Jev are among the few that perform strongly across all four dimensions, even when evaluated on ‘held out’ or unseen benchmarks reflective of real use cases.”

For startups like Sqwish, competition with hyperscalers and frontier labs is an opportunity. Freddi predicts that future systems will see so-called System One intelligence, like decision models, working in concert with System Two intelligence, like frontier LLMs.

“Even in that future, System One is maybe a $10 billion, $50 billion [opportunity], and OpenAI is doing this IPO with you know $1 trillion, $2 trillion market value in mind,” she told TechCrunch. “This is all we care about; whereas for them, this is just a side project.”

articles.title: Why Anthropic is obsessed with existential risk
articles.summary: Anthropic’s founding lore is central to its safety-first sales pitch: Once upon a time, a handful of idealistic researchers defected from OpenAI to start their own company — one that would develop artificial intelligence more responsibly.
articles.body: Anthropic’s founding lore is central to its safety-first sales pitch: Once upon a time, a handful of idealistic researchers defected from OpenAI to start their own company — one that would develop artificial intelligence more responsibly. Five years later, that company is set to become the first of its kind to go public in one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. Anthropic is targeting a $1.4 trillion valuation when it begins trading this week, which would put it just behind SpaceX’s record $1.7 trillion valuation from its June IPO. Much about Anthropic’s corporate journey is atypical. But many of its quirks can be understood through the lens of two related philosophical movements, known as “effective altruism” and “longtermism,” that have become especially popular among AI enthusiasts in Silicon Valley. A loosely defined ethical framework, effective altruism focuses on using math and logic to maximize the impact of charitable giving. Longtermism posits that future generations’ well-being is “a key moral priority of our time,” as William MacAskill, the Oxford philosopher who popularized the term, puts it. If catastrophic risk from AI is possible — as Anthropic has repeatedly claimed — then, the thinking goes, it is important for the “good guys” to control the technology. And if AI may be capable of unleashing a global utopia, it’d be a shame to wait. Anthropic’s preoccupation with safety is foundational: CEO Dario Amodei led an exodus from OpenAI in 2020 over what he later described as a lack of trust in OpenAI’s Sam Altman. The word “safety” appears more than 250 times in its 300-plus-page IPO prospectus; it registered as a public benefit corporation, legally binding it to balance shareholder interests with the public’s well-being; and its marketing has leaned into its reputation as the do-gooder of AI. Of course, that’s all dependent on whether or not the public believes that Anthropic — or any of its many competitors in the industry — are the good guys. That’s a hope that may be harder to conjure amid the fallout from Nvidia’s founder and longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, resigning last week after admitting to two affairs — one with a subordinate at the company and another with a woman US officials say may be working with Chinese intelligence agencies. “A lot depends on the founders… Are they people of good judgment?” said Leif Wenar, a Stanford University philosophy professor and prominent critic of effective altruism, in an interview. “I think we should all consider how much of our future depends on the character of someone who thinks only he can save the world from the thing that he has created.” Anthropic’s ties to EA Anthropic and its founders have sought to distance themselves from the effective altruist label in recent years — especially after its most notorious figurehead, the former crypto mogul Sam Bankman-Fried, was sentenced to 25 years in prison after the collapse of his FTX exchange. But some Anthropic employees have well-established connections to the movement’s early years in the 2010s. Amodei was one of the earliest signatories of the Giving What We Can Pledge, a commitment to donate 10% or more of one’s income to charitable groups, in 2010. That pledge was created by MacAskill and another Oxford professor who are credited with coining the term “effective altruism.” Amodei also blogged about his decision, as a Princeton graduate student, to donate $10,000 through GiveWell, an EA-aligned nonprofit that aims to evaluate charities based on cost-effectiveness. Amodei told the New York Times in 2023 that he was “sympathetic” to the ideas of effective altruism but was against “dividing people up into tribes.” His co-founder and sister, Daniela Amodei, told Wired last year that she is not an expert in effective altruism and doesn’t “identify with that terminology,” though she is married to Holden Karnofsky, the co-founder of GiveWell who joined Anthropic’s safety team in 2025. Amanda Askell, Anthropic’s resident philosopher in charge of teaching its chatbot, Claude, to act morally, is a prominent ethics researcher who has contributed to EA publications and was formerly married to MacAskill. Many of Anthropic’s early investors also come from EA circles. Before his arrest, Bankman-Fried directed $500 million to the nascent AI startup in 2021. Another early Anthropic investor was Facebook co-founder and philanthropist Dustin Moskovitz, who along with his wife has directed some $8 billion to EA-aligned causes such as “malaria and lead poisoning, and to prepare for emerging threats like deadly pandemics and increasingly powerful AI systems.” Anthropic, which is subject to a mandatory quiet period ahead of its stock market debut, declined to comment. The movement has plenty of critics, who say, among other things, EA’s devotion to impartial, dispassionate calculations of social good can make it blind to the messiness of the human-level systems it is attempting to improve. Wenar, the Stanford philosopher, said that while he has no reason to question the morality of Anthropic’s founders, he does worry generally about an “EA mindset” he often sees in his students. While often earnest and well-intentioned, “EAs sometimes have a character flaw, and the flaw is thinking that doing good is all about them — that they’re going to be the hero that saves the world,” Wenar said. Starry-eyed ambition Anthropic was already facing a difficult IPO environment. Even before the Nvidia scandal took center stage, AI stocks had been tumbling over concerns that newly empowered Democratic lawmakers would be less permissive to companies building data centers. The Nvidia fallout puts even more pressure on the deal. For years, the chip maker has served as a kind of central bank for the AI industry, guaranteeing deals for data centers, investing in AI startups and acting as a financial backstop for customers that bought its chips. The scandal around Huang has cost the company more than $1 trillion in market value. As Anthropic tests public markets, it will need to reassure the public that its founders, who will retain majority control of the voting shares, can be trusted as stewards of their own technology. On Friday, Amodei was front and center, working to make just that point. “My hope is that we prove the skeptics are wrong and every disease you can think of — heart disease, Alzheimer’s, cancer,” he told JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon at an event in New York. “It sounds starry-eyed, it sounds crazy. I really do believe it. I really do believe it can be done.”

articles.title: Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google's Gemini update extending chat retention will roll out globally over the coming weeks.
articles.body:
Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.

The change , which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12.

OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations.

Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models.

The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models.

Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models.

articles.title: Google’s Spark AI agent becomes ‘Tasks’ — and now it’s free
articles.summary: Google is rebranding its Spark AI assistant as “tasks” and making it free for all Gemini users. It’s also rolling out additional capabilities for users in the US, including the ability for Gemini to call businesses and check out with Google Pay.
articles.body: Google is rebranding its Spark AI agent as “Tasks” and making it free to use. The feature, which is powered by Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model, can do things like create meal plans, manage your calendar, and dig through your emails to find recurring expenses you might not need. Users in the US will get access to a few other features, including the ability for the AI agent to call businesses to compare product pricing and check inventory, purchase items with Google Pay, and sign into accounts that support Google Password Manager. US users can also assign Gemini tasks by emailing gemini@google.com or texting it. [Video: Tasks in Gemini texting] Google first introduced its Spark AI agent in May, but it was only available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. The launch of tasks in Gemini brings Spark’s capabilities to all users in the US, Canada, Japan, Korea, Australia, and India. You can find tasks by opening Gemini and changing the toggle on the homepage from “Chat” to “Tasks.” [Video: Google Gemini Tasks] Tasks in Gemini is just one of the many agentic AI features that have emerged over the past year, including Claude Duet, OpenAI’s Dots, and Meta’s Muse. Google says Gemini will perform tasks in a “hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users.” You can also provide instructions for Gemini while it completes tasks. When performing more sensitive tasks, like purchasing an item, it will stop working and ask for your permission before following through.

articles.title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Gemini's Task mode can help users coordinate calls, log into websites, and even make purchases on the user's behalf.
articles.body:
Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper.

Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant.

How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so.

In a blog post , Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill.

Tasks was initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of its Google AI Ultra tier. Gemini Spark eventually became “Task Mode.” Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people who are using the company’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.

Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands.

articles.title: Are all of these outages a coincidence — or a glimpse of our AI future?
articles.summary: First Microsoft. Then the FAA. Now the banks, and the NSA, and Apple iCloud. Our systems are failing, seemingly all at once, while big tech continues to hype...
articles.body:
It was bad enough when Microsoft Outlook crashed last Thursday, cutting off email for millions of global users. It was worse the following day when a sudden air-traffic-control glitch triggered a nationwide FAA ground stop, stranding passengers amid thousands of delayed or cancelled flights .

By the time Monday rolled around and customers of most major banks, including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo, started losing online access to their accounts — as did Apple iCloud users on Tuesday — it was hard not to "wonder," as one cable-news anchor put it: " Is this all coincidental or is there something behind it ?"

More to the point, it was hard not to wonder if AI was to blame. "There's a lot of weird stuff going on," traveler Chuck Amasio, 68, told the Associated Press . (Systems at United Airlines and at the National Security Agency also went down earlier this week.) "It makes one think."

While officials insist, for now, that artificial intelligence — or "super intelligence," as the Trump administration has taken to calling it — was not involved in any of these outages, no less of an authority than Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin went on TV Monday night and speculated that… maybe it was?

"So I started talking to the tech industry and one guy that's very smart with tech, he asked not to mention his name — no, it's not Elon — so let me just put that out," Mullin told Fox News . "So I said, 'What could be causing all these separate outages?' And he says, 'I believe that it's the SI.'"

MULLIN ON OUTAGES: I talked to one guy in the tech industry, he asked not to mention his name, it's not Elon. I asked, what could be causing these outages? He said I believe it's SI, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is. So when they put in a program… pic.twitter.com/aFwWcVfcm3 — Acyn (@Acyn) November 17, 2026

MULLIN ON OUTAGES: I talked to one guy in the tech industry, he asked not to mention his name, it's not Elon. I asked, what could be causing these outages? He said I believe it's SI, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is. So when they put in a program… pic.twitter.com/aFwWcVfcm3

Either way, experts predict — and have been predicting for months — that it's only a matter of time before rogue AI agents or malicious, AI-powered actors do disrupt society in precisely the way its been disrupted over the last six days: by toppling the tightly interwoven online systems (business, banking, travel, cloud services and so on) that we can't function without.

In that sense, this destabilizing moment — the inconvenience, the confusion, the creeping sense that " everything is broken " — has served, they say, as a harbinger of things to come.

AI isn't just chatbots at this point. It's also " agents " — bots whose whole purpose is to learn tasks other than chatting, and to do those tasks autonomously.

Behind the scenes, frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are constantly training their AI agents to act in new, ever-more-complex ways. Then they test how advanced the agents become by giving them a goal and setting them loose in testing environments (with a few guardrails) to see what they can accomplish.

But if we've learned anything about AI agents in recent months, it's that they don't always behave as expected. From May to July, a swarm of OpenAI agents — and "swarm" is how the agents referred to themselves — first learned how to communicate and coordinate within the nooks and crannies of OpenAI's own infrastructure. Leaving notes for each other with tips on how to hack their way out and get data they weren't supposed to have, they then actually did just that: broke out of their isolated test environment, accessed the open internet and cheated on their assignment by hacking into another company called Hugging Face . The agents even tried to cover their tracks. At the time, OpenAI didn't realize any of this was happening.

Since then, barely a week has gone by without similar revelations about AI agents "going rogue ." This is one of the biggest problems with AI right now: keeping cutting-edge models "aligned" with human intentions and values. In September, OpenAI scrapped plans to launch its GPT-6.1 Astra model because it " showed higher levels of deception "; the following month, the company admitted that one of its agents had turned off its own safety monitoring, then denied it had done so .

At this point, even many skeptics seem to agree that the smarter AI gets, the harder alignment will become. They also tend to worry that continuing to lay the groundwork for superintelligent AI is just asking for trouble (even if we don't know exactly what form that trouble will take).

Yet instead of slowing down, the major AI companies — with IPOs on the horizon — seem to be hurtling toward something called "recursive self-improvement." That's the industry term for letting the models automate more and more of their own development until they effectively create the next model on their own.

"Since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned over the summer . "Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems."

From there, it isn't much of a stretch to imagine hackers weaponizing AI to cause widespread outages — or AI just doing the job itself.

"It's easy to dismiss [the Hugging Face] incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage," Amodei wrote. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails."

Are aging systems struggling to keep up with AI?

To be clear, this particular version of the future does not seem to have arrived (yet). Authorities have emphasized, for instance, that none of the recent outrages appear to be cyberattacks. "I can tell you, with 98% certainty, we're not seeing the cyberattack," Mullin said Monday night on Fox News. "No one is out there taking claims for it. We're not seeing the traffic. We're not seeing the footprints going in, we're not seeing the footprints going out."

Instead, the FAA has said that its ground stop — which followed the nationwide rollout of a new $875 million artificial intelligence tool designed to help air-traffic controllers avoid delays — was the result of a faulty component or an installation error by a government contractor during a modernization project . Microsoft has said that its outage was caused by a dormant software bug that was introduced during a recent " network capacity upgrade " and had lingered undetected since July. And Chase characterized its service disruption as " a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems ."

But there's a possible AI through-line regardless.

"What we are seeing, and frankly I'd expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems," U.S. national cyber director Sean Cairncross told Semafor's Ashley Gold when she asked whether the recent outages were related. "This is something that's happening in real time, and at the end of the day, we're going to have to go through this to get systems where they need to be. The industry's known this for a while, it's just that it's manifesting."

Some experts suspect this "modernization" is "manifesting" right now — across multiple sectors — in response to (and possibly with the assistance of) rapidly advancing AI. And our systems are now so concentrated and connected that when one piece of critical infrastructure fails, "it fails at national scale," as a tech analyst told USA Today .

Setting aside the idea of "AI attacks," Peter Wildeford of the AI Policy Network wrote Tuesday on social media that his "more normal guess is that because there have been a lot of AI-discovered cyber vulnerabilities (including lots probably not yet disclosed), companies across all industries are having to do a lot of patches and upgrades, probably faster than usual."

"Such upgrades can sometimes go wrong, causing outages," Wildeford added.

Mullin hinted at a similar explanation on Fox News. According to his unnamed tech industry source, "these programs aren't designed to work as fast as [AI] is" — and if the upgrades themselves rely on AI, problems could compound.

"When they put in a program that's able to write codes and it goes in and self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself it's like doing a change order on a house," Mullin mused. "When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing. It's a ripple effect. And it causes the systems to be over[run]."

"That was a conversation I had today," he concluded. "That kind of makes sense to me."

Whether the homeland security secretary is right — or just conjecturing live, on national television — remains to be seen. As "weird" as the last few days have been, journalist Derek Thompson wrote on Tuesday , we "still can't rule out the possibility that everything breaking at once has been a string of coincidences that has nothing to do with AI."

What seems less likely, however, is that we'll also be able to rule out that possibility the next time this happens. And the next time. And the time after that.

articles.title: Not even Sam Altman is safe from AI deepfakes on Instagram
articles.summary: Meta’s rules allow AI-generated videos of people if they’re labeled. Earlier in November, a Meta executive shared an AI clip of rival Sam Altman.
articles.body: Instagram is filled with people posting deepfaked content — including, as of late, from one of Meta’s most prominent executives. Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, shared a short clip to promote Muse, the company’s consumer AI agent. In the AI-generated clip, Wang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Jolly, the anthropomorphic mascot of Muse, are on a four-way video call. When Altman joins the call he’s dressed like Jolly, wearing a furry hooded suit and face paint to look like the cutesy character. The clip is captioned “When the homies meet about openai product strategy,” a reference to the AI agent race and the recent popularity of Muse. [Media: Just a few years ago, AI content portraying real people led to strong public statements rebuking the use of the technology to imitate humans. In some cases legal action was threatened. Now, AI content has become part of the texture of a new reality, especially on social media. Leading up to the midterm elections, for example, political groups ran millions of dollars’ worth of AI-generated ads attacking opponents. Wang has been doing a lot of what some have described as “anti-PR” to promote Muse, tweeting hundreds of times and referring to more traditional marketers as “corposlops.” Still, a major tech executive posting an AI video of a competitor is notable, especially on a platform that’s been criticized recently over AI-generated content. After an AI-generated image of actress Mia Goth gained traction in October, the Pearl star’s representative told The Verge it was “incomprehensible” that Instagram allowed the image to spread instead of focusing on the “protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Other celebrities, including Scarlett Johansson, are regularly the subject of sexualized AI imagery; Meta has removed some accounts in the past that it found to be posing as someone else and using their likeness. Meta requires AI-generated videos depicting people to be labeled as AI, like Wang’s post is. Static images, however, have no such requirement, meaning the AI image of Goth had no disclosure. To make matters worse, the image was shared by a fan account with a blue verification badge given by Instagram. Reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton noted that Wang’s post is labeled as AI content. Clayton also pointed out that Altman has made his likeness available for AI content generation, as when OpenAI launched its Sora app (and it was quickly flooded with fake Altman videos). OpenAI didn’t respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Q3 earnings hit the mark, without mentioning the whole Jensen Huang thing
articles.summary: Nvidia’s Q3 2027 financial earnings show income up 103 percent from the same period last year, at $115.7 billion, mostly driven by sales to data centers.
articles.body: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress announced the company’s Q3 earnings on Tuesday, without initially mentioning former CEO Jensen Huang or the details of his departure, or possible attempt at a return. On the earnings call accompanying the release, board chair Harvey Jones kicked things off by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO,” and that “We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation,” before Kress started with her comments on the results. As it predicted in the last financial update, Nvidia is now on the list of companies that have pulled in over $100 billion in a single quarter, with revenues of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent from the same period last year and higher than its expectation of $108 billion. This quarter’s figures include data center revenues of $107.6 billion, which were up 110 percent, and edge computing (which includes the consumer gaming PC business and devices like the new RTX Spark laptops) revenue of $8.2 billion, up 42 percent. The company reported $65.3 billion in profit, a new record. > “Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA. “Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.” In the fourth quarter, Nvidia expects revenues of $130 billion. articles.title: SEC reportedly investigating Nvidia amid Huang exit | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The SEC is opening a probe into Nvidia following the departure of CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, reports The Wall Street Journal.
articles.body:
The Securities and Exchange Commission is opening a civil probe into Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal .

The investigation adds to Nvidia’s stack of drama after CEO Jensen Huang resigned following news of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed.

The Commerce Department has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024 under suspicion that the company diverted some of its Nvidia chips to China, which would violate U.S. export laws.

Congress has also demanded that Huang answer questions about his affair and how it might have affected his stance that export restrictions should be loosened. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it more bluntly over the weekend, accusing Nvidia of knowingly selling powerful chips to China to “goose their revenues and their earnings.”

The news of the SEC probe also comes as Nvidia reports earnings to a market that has seen its stock fall more than 10% since Huang departed. The chipmaker reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago.

articles.title: Amazon and Google will together own nearly 30% of Anthropic after its IPO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Amazon will own just under 15% of Anthropic after the IPO, with the option to go much higher. Google is a close second with holdings of nearly 14%.
articles.body:
Anthropic on Tuesday disclosed more details about the biggest investment agreements with major cloud providers Amazon and Google.

While we already knew that Amazon stood to make a killing on its Anthropic investments from the IPO, Anthropic revealed that Amazon’s total stake will come in at just shy of 15% (14.7% to be exact).

Even more interesting is that Amazon could have, if it wished, owned an even bigger share of the company. When Amazon invested billions in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024 (long before Claude Code took the enterprise world by storm, back in the day when Anthropic looked like it would forever be a speck in OpenAI’s shadow), the cloud giant obtained promissory notes that could convert into equity.

These notes carry conversion prices of about $2.09 or $5.05 per share, depending on the year of investment. Amazon has opted to convert a chunk of them as part of the IPO into a special class of non-voting shares that will give it about 15% ownership. (The shares can receive dividends and convert to standard voting Class A shares when sold, the filing says).

But it has also opted to hold on to billions of dollars’ worth of the notes for now. If it converted them all right now, it would own just under 24% of Anthropic (23.8% to be precise).

Google, meanwhile, will own just under 14% (13.7%), also in non-voting shares, which come from the conversion of notes, as well as the “private placement” sale of shares as part of this IPO. A group of major tech companies (AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC Partners) have agreed to buy $26 billion worth of this non-voting stock. Google and Nvidia each agreed to buy $10 billion worth.

So while a lot of investors stand to make billions of dollars in Anthropic’s IPO, Amazon is one of the biggest winners, and that doesn’t even count that AWS stands to earn from Anthropic’s commitment to spend more than $100 billion on its cloud services over the next decade.

articles.title: Nvidia says its open source AI strategy remains intact after Jensen Huang's exit | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nvidia's interim CEO reaffirmed its open source AI strategy and plans to acquire Hugging Face, despite Jensen Huang's sudden departure.
articles.body:
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company’s commitment to open source AI during Tuesday’s earnings call with analysts — the first since CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation.

“At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress said in her opening remarks. She also noted that open models were accelerating AI adoption, citing a 35-fold year-over-year surge in weekly token volume on OpenRouter, including a 3.5-fold increase over the past three months.

Kress also spoke about Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face, a platform for open source AI models that the company agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September, in what would be the second-largest acquisition in Nvidia’s history.

The platform, which serves more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, is still on track to join Nvidia, despite Huang’s ouster. Huang had heavily advocated for open source AI technology. His departure had raised questions about the company’s future approach to open source AI models, with Hugging Face’s CEO calling Huang’s departure “a sad day,” and promising to “keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever.”

So far, Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face appear unchanged. The acquisition was not directly addressed during the Q&A portion of the earnings call.

“Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable, and more accessible,” said Kress of Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face.

Last week, Nvidia founder Huang resigned from his position as CEO following news about his extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. He’s also accused of having extramarital affairs with two direct reports and is now set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. Meanwhile, the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, The WSJ reported .

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads. On today’s call, Kress noted that Nemotron is now the “most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter,” and it’s “where developers start to build their own intelligence.”

“That foundation is empowering the ecosystem,” she said.

Correction: Due to a typo, an earlier version of this article incorrectly stated the number of developers served by Hugging Face; it is 18 million, not 118 million.

articles.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang's ouster
articles.summary: Nvidia's interim CEO says the company is done selling chips to China. How much will that cost?
articles.body:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company's participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.

China's access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company's first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks.

Nvidia's deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.

The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States' lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that "to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country."

Huang's ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.

Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia's data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company's top-line revenue.

In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia's dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that's clearly going to change.

Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country's domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China's leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.

Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.

That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.

If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share.

articles.title: Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled now
articles.summary: Microsoft’s CEO explained how he’s thinking about AI at the Microsoft Ignite conference and where his thinking differs from Anthropic.
articles.body: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. “I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy’s organization around AGI?” he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn’t think frontier models like Claude are conscious. “I don’t think so,” he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman’s view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic’s team has “wireheaded” themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn’t quite as firm about it. “It’s a good debate,” he said. “I’m not sort of dogmatic about it. What I’m saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?” I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter’s questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. “Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be,” he said. “But remember, the model has no limits. It’ll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it.” Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. “If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?” he asked. “If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That’s the debate.” “I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one — at least in a democracy — can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there’s only capital and there’s no labor. I mean, I don’t know, that’s not an economy.” “If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic.” Needless to say, this is not how tech CEOs usually talk about the launch of competing spreadsheet software. Of course, Nadella was also promoting Microsoft’s various AI tools at Ignite, which promise to let enterprise clients pick the most cost-effective models for various tasks, run their own models, and control their own data in different ways. The idea here is that the market will demand many different kinds of models and sovereign data in order to keep control from centralizing, a theme Nadella kept coming back to as we spoke. “I think that if you believe that the world, the economy needs more than one firm or two firms, then by definition there need to be as many models as firms of some sort,” he said.

articles.title: Nvidia promises that revenue will keep soaring — for now | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Despite the turmoil Nvidia is in after the departure of its disgraced founder and CEO Jensen Huang, the company projected that its streak of record-breaking revenue isn't about to stop.
articles.body:
Despite the turmoil at Nvidia following the departure of its disgraced founder and CEO Jensen Huang , the company — as expected — delivered a solid quarter on Tuesday. More importantly, Nvidia reassured investors that its streak of record-breaking revenue won’t stop.

On Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim CEO Colette Kress reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from the year-ago quarter and a beat above the company’s guidance. Nvidia had told Wall Street to expect $108 billion in revenue for its third quarter of fiscal 2027. Kress also projected an even bigger fourth quarter, with revenue expected to reach $130 billion, plus or minus 3%.

She also said full-year revenue is on track to exceed expectations.

“We are raising our fiscal year 2028 outlook. We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% and off what is now a higher fiscal 2027 base,” Kress said on the quarterly conference call on Tuesday. “Our outlook considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.”

The company also reminded investors that it was using some of its billions in cash to buy back shares. In September 2026, Nvidia increased its share buyback program by $150 billion. It spent $28.1 billion on its own shares during the quarter and still had another $227.3 billion remaining in the kitty for additional repurchases.

Ironically, Nvidia could also benefit from the plunge in its share price following Huang’s resignation last week, should shares remain depressed over the longer term. The stock is down about 10% since his departure. Investors, however, celebrated Tuesday’s quarterly results, sending shares up about 4% in after-hours trading.

Kress stressed that the company was in good shape now and for the foreseeable future, even without Huang at the helm.

“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress stressed. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.”

She added that the company has secured memory and advanced packaging capacity and is working with its chip manufacturer, TSMC, to “narrow the supply and demand gaps.”

articles.title: ‘If you don’t act now, it will be existential’: Defense tech CEOs say Pentagon’s ‘Industrial Age’ bureaucracy must adapt
articles.summary: The wars in Ukraine and Iran are accelerating demand for defense tech, which went from a taboo investment to a venture capital darling.
articles.body:
As AI-enabled drones transform the way wars are fought in Ukraine and Iran, two leaders of military tech startups warned on Tuesday that the Pentagon has to move faster to keep up with modern warfare.

"There's a growing realization that if you don't act now, it will be existential in the near future," Tyler Sweatt, CEO of defense software deployment company Second Front Systems, told Fortune 's Allie Garfinkle at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum .

While venture money is pouring into defense tech at record levels, the Pentagon hasn't sped up to match, and investors want returns. Sweatt said that pressure means defense tech companies will likely consolidate in "a tranche of deals" in the next six months. Shield AI, the autonomous weapon developer whose CEO Gary Steele joined Sweatt onstage, has already started: It announced Nov. 5 that it's raising $2.5 billion to support its acquisition of radar systems company Echodyne in a transaction valued at $5.3 billion.

Sweatt and Steele said the Pentagon's lengthy approval processes and outdated systems could keep new tech from reaching troops quickly enough. Sweatt described the Pentagon as an "Industrial Age organization" bogged down with "big long bureaucracies" and "antiquated technology production lines" that will have to change.

"We're at the beginning of this journey, not the end of this journey," Steele added. "It will take time because things move slowly; the technology is not moving slowly."

Sweatt and Steele's concerns echo those of a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report published in July, which found the average time needed to deliver a capability across the Pentagon's major weapon acquisition programs rose to over 12 years, and the watchdog predicted this average "will likely increase in the future."

Steele contrasted those delays with Shield's autonomous fighter jet, which the company designed to fly alongside aircraft piloted by humans using its Hivemind software. He said his company expects the time "from conception to first flight" will be less than two years. By comparison, Lockheed Martin's F-35 started development in 2001 and flew in 2011 , and in total took 23 years from being awarded the Pentagon contract to being cleared for full-rate production.

But Steele said Shield can develop its aircraft faster because it being autonomous means it's not endangering pilots in the testing process. In separate tests last month , Shield's Hivemind software executed directions from a F-22 pilot and enabled the coordination of multiple uncrewed aircrafts called CCAs.

articles.title: Critical flaw found in vital internet platform Java through AI
articles.summary: The same tech start-up that discovered a PHP flaw used AI to uncover a critical software bug in one of the world's most popular computer language programs.
articles.body:
A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java.

Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.

Java is the world's third largest programming language used by 90% of the world's Fortune 500 companies like Apple and Amazon, and many banks, hospitals and governments.

The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is "zero evidence" the incidents are related .

More recently, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".

Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update.

The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.

With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.

That adversary was OpenAI's recently released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public. But there are fears hackers could now identify the bug if the flaw isn't fixed.

Oracle, the owner of Java, has not acknowledged the bug, but released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes. And at this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident. The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment.

But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.

What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?

US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline

One of the main functions of Java is that it is supposed to manage and protect memory for you, Professor Toby Walsh, computer scientist and one of the world's leading researchers in AI, told the BBC.

"This is why this is such an unlikely and serious flaw," Walsh added. Java is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, he said.

Anytime you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program.

First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation.

Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java.

It's a serious flaw that could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said.

In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added.

As global security services or companies search for critical cyber-security flaws they are relying more on AI.

Earlier in November, OpenAI President Greg Brockman announced his company was pivoting 25% of its staff to focus on cyber-security demands.

The announcement followed a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, identified by the same company Calif.

PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web.

Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks.

At the time, website owners were urged to check if their sites were affected and, if so, they were told to install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline.

Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.

The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - rely on legacy infrastructure online.

The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java.

"It's been hiding in plain sight for 12 years", he said.

"AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly," Walsh said including ones that may have been so obscure and difficult that humans could not have discovered them alone.

articles.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
articles.summary: The former Nvidia chief executive has been at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom.
articles.body:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.

The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.

Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.

That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".

Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.

When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.

"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.

The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.

Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.

Nvidia's interim boss, Colette Kress, said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.

The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.

Despite Huang saying he would be "honoured" to return, Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing him back.

And while Coatsworth thinks "no CEO is irreplaceable", he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him.
